of 50 million `new Pair(left, right)` operations repeatedly entered
`construct`, `construct_dispatch`, `run_constructor_on`, and `call_user`, even though the class had
no fields, private members, decorator initializers, or derived `super()` setup. Two million such
constructions took several times as long as the direct and method-call controls.

## Optimization

Fieldless base classes can now enter the existing identity-cached JIT constructor path. The
constructor-only cache records this eligibility after validating the class metadata. Derived
classes and classes with fields, private members, or decorator initializers continue through the
full class-construction path.

GC polling, argument ownership transfer, reflective frame, `this` and `new.target` setup,
exception propagation, return override, and tail-call drain. It also clears and restores the
derived-constructor `super()` permission around the base-class body, matching
`run_constructor_on`.

The focused benchmark is `crates/lumen/benches/call_dispatch.js`. Seven fresh-process rounds were
rotated between clean release builds of `f887240` and this change on Apple Silicon. Values are
medians in milliseconds; lower is better.

| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Stable direct calls | 43 | 43 | 0% |
| Stable method calls | 46 | 46 | 0% |
| Fieldless base-class construction | 257 | 97 | -62% |
| Stable native calls | 44 | 44 | 0% |
| Recursive-call control | 10 | 11 | timer-level noise |

This audit starts from `origin/main` at `b0f9b75` and follows the constructor work already merged
in PR #26. It covers native builtins, bound functions, `call`/`apply`, trailing spread calls, and
remaining polymorphic call helpers. It does not change closure dispatch.

The focused matrix is `crates/lumen/benches/call_dispatch_matrix.js`. It executes two million
operations for each direct-native, four-way native and user-polymorphic, bound-user,
bound-native, user/native `call`, user/native `apply`, and user/native spread shape.

Diagnostic counters on the unmodified base reported 4,060,025 native call-IC entries and
4,060,000 `CallSpreadThis` helper entries. A native sample of the matrix's spread phase was
dominated by `Interp::call_dispatch`, `Interp::iterator_step`, Array Iterator `next`, property-map
work, and iterator-result object construction. The ordinary four-way call IC was already active;
`Function.prototype.call` and dense-array `apply` already had dedicated JIT paths. Bound calls
were slower than direct calls, but their target and bound-argument reconstruction did not offer a
comparably narrow semantics-safe change. Dense trailing spread was the clear outlier at about two
seconds per two million calls.

The JIT slow helper now scalar-replaces a complete Array Iterator walk for arrays of at most 16
elements when all of these guards hold:

- the spread value is an ordinary, plain Array with an own data `length`;
- every visited element is an own data property, with no holes or accessors;
- `@@iterator` is the active realm's original `Array.prototype.values` by identity; and
- the active realm's Array Iterator `next` is still the original function by identity.

Any miss is side-effect-free and runs the prior iterator protocol unchanged. This keeps proxies,
custom iterators, getters, inherited holes, mutated iterator methods, and foreign-realm
intrinsics on the observable path. A hit still enters one logical recursion-limit and amortized
GC-poll boundary for `values`, every yielded `next`, and the final done-producing `next`. The
eventual target continues through the existing call path, preserving callable and proxy identity,
receiver handling, argument order and ownership, target exceptions, reflective frames, tail
calls, and target recursion/GC behavior.

function sharing its caller's live, non-global lexical environment. It is off by

The first implemented pass is backward local liveness over the existing target-neutral
control-flow graph (`jit_ir/liveness.rs`). ARM64 local-load lowering transfers ownership
at proven last uses, avoiding a clone and the original slot's eventual drop. The source
slot becomes `undefined`; the normal TDZ check still runs before the transfer. This
works for every value representation, including BigInt.

The analysis joins successor live sets and iterates to a fixed point across backedges.
Unknown instructions keep all slots live. Captured/aliased frames, exception handlers,
frames above 128 slots and chunks above 4096 instructions are excluded. Failure to
converge within the compile-time budget also declines the optimization. Other native
regions continue using their existing emitters; this pass does not replace their
register allocation or introduce speculative deoptimization.

Set `LUMEN_JIT_NO_LAST_USES=1` to disable the pass for comparison. `LUMEN_JIT_FAST`
continues to control local-load lowering through its existing bit 3.

## Initial evidence

On Apple M4, preliminary three-round comparisons with the same release executable,
alternating the pass on and off, were effectively flat:

| Workload | Disabled median | Enabled median |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 5000 DeltaBlue iterations | 9802 ms | 9758 ms |
| 10000 Djot parse/render iterations | 6064 ms | 6047 ms |

These differences are within noise, and some runs overlapped development compilation; the shared machine also had unrelated
compiler activity.
They are not evidence of an application speedup. A quiet rerun is required before
making any performance claim. The pass is an initial reusable optimization, not the
completed milestone of improving both DeltaBlue and a real application substantially.

Five-second native sampling showed reference-counting, allocation and cycle collection
in both workloads. Djot additionally executes significant AST-interpreter work; its
hot-function log includes arrows reading lexical `this`, class constructors and renderer
methods. Sampling does not by itself establish how much any proposed change will save.

The next work needs to address those costs: broaden compilation coverage for real
application functions, then use shared IR facts for register-resident values and guarded
inlining across operations. Heap work should be guided by measured collector/allocation
costs. Keep the interpreter as the semantic oracle throughout.

## Reproducing the parser workload

From the repository root:

```sh
(cd examples/djot-parser && npm ci --ignore-scripts)
bun build examples/djot-parser/bench.mjs --target=browser --format=iife --outfile=/tmp/lumen-djot.js
cargo build --release -p lumen --bin lumen
LUMEN_JIT_NO_LAST_USES=1 target/release/lumen --tier=jit /tmp/lumen-djot.js
target/release/lumen --tier=jit /tmp/lumen-djot.js
node /tmp/lumen-djot.js
bun /tmp/lumen-djot.js

The bundle isolates engine execution from module-loader differences. Bun is only a
benchmark build tool. Every iteration verifies the complete rendered HTML against the
reference output. The timer includes tier warmup but excludes initial bundle loading.
Run engines sequentially, alternate ordering and compare several fresh processes.

- Three public-boundary ownership tests passed in all three execution tiers.
- Differential fuzzing: 1996 agreeing programs, four skipped for resource budgets.

that binding when it is read, using the interpreter's shared resolver. It does not bind
`this` from the arrow's caller or eagerly read a derived constructor's uninitialized
binding. Nested arrows forward the original binding through their environment chain.
Receiver-direct property operations remain reserved for ordinary function receivers.

Three fresh-process rounds, alternating engine order and without concurrent development
builds, produced these medians (milliseconds, lower is better):

| Workload | Before | After | Node 24.18.0 | Bun 1.3.14 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Djot, 10000 verified parse/render iterations | 6149 | 5705 | 235 | 145 |
| DeltaBlue, 5000 iterations | 10003 | 9872 | 205 | 315 |

dynamic-import failure. Strict Clippy still reports the existing 86/88 errors outside

discriminant, initializes every case's `let`/`const` to TDZ before testing cases, and
preserves fallthrough, default placement and outer-loop control flow. The lowering is
extracted into `bytecode/switch.rs`.

unsupported `for…in` loop. Its three-round median stayed flat (5541 ms before, 5546 ms
after). Compiled enumeration is the next coverage dependency; no renderer speedup is
claimed from switch support alone.

From the repository root:

```sh
(cd examples/djot-parser && npm ci --ignore-scripts)
bun build examples/djot-parser/bench.mjs --target=browser --format=iife --outfile=/tmp/lumen-djot.js
cargo build --release -p lumen --bin lumen
LUMEN_JIT_NO_LAST_USES=1 target/release/lumen --tier=jit /tmp/lumen-djot.js
target/release/lumen --tier=jit /tmp/lumen-djot.js
node /tmp/lumen-djot.js
bun /tmp/lumen-djot.js
```

The bundle isolates engine execution from module-loader differences. Bun is only a
benchmark build tool. Every iteration verifies the complete rendered HTML against the
reference output. The timer includes tier warmup but excludes initial bundle loading.
Run engines sequentially, alternate ordering and compare several fresh processes.

- 603 engine unit tests passed, including five new liveness tests.
- Three public-boundary ownership tests passed in all three execution tiers.
- Differential fuzzing: 1996 agreeing programs, four skipped for resource budgets.

- Formatting and strict structure checks on the new modules passed. Strict Clippy
  remains blocked by 86 library / 88 library-test pre-existing errors; no new module
  diagnostics were reported.

## Lexical-this compilation

Arrow functions that read lexical `this` now compile. The new bytecode operation resolves
that binding when it is read, using the interpreter's shared resolver. It does not bind
`this` from the arrow's caller or eagerly read a derived constructor's uninitialized
binding. Nested arrows forward the original binding through their environment chain.
Receiver-direct property operations remain reserved for ordinary function receivers.

builds, produced these medians (milliseconds, lower is better):

| Workload | Before | After | Node 24.18.0 | Bun 1.3.14 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Djot, 10000 verified parse/render iterations | 6149 | 5705 | 235 | 145 |
| DeltaBlue, 5000 iterations | 10003 | 9872 | 205 | 315 |

discriminant, initializes every case's `let`/`const` to TDZ before testing cases, and

extracted into `bytecode/switch.rs`.

unsupported `for…in` loop. Its three-round median stayed flat (5541 ms before, 5546 ms
after). Compiled enumeration is the next coverage dependency; no renderer speedup is
claimed from switch support alone.

module. The module passes the strict structure audit.

`for…in` loops with uncaptured `let`/`const` identifier heads now compile. Key snapshots
use the interpreter's shared namespace/prototype enumeration implementation; stepping
rechecks property presence to skip deleted keys. Hidden frame slots retain the base,
private key snapshot and cursor. No user array iterator is invoked. Captured loop heads
retain their per-iteration environments through the interpreter. SSA regions explicitly
decline the new cursor-writing operation until that local effect is modeled.

This completes the two compilation dependencies for Djot's main renderer. Three-round
medians were 5587 ms before and 5182 ms after (about 7% less time), versus Node 227 ms
and Bun 143 ms. The parser entry still falls back because of a captured default parameter.

tests passed. The sole conformance failure is the previously reproduced dynamic import

## Captured literal defaults

Captured parameters can now use primitive literals or empty object/array defaults. The
initializer writes the captured binding only for an absent/undefined argument. Defaults
with effects or parameter-scope dependencies, and same-name hoisted-function conflicts,
remain on the interpreter. Existing uncaptured-default analysis moved into
`bytecode/parameters.rs` alongside the new initialization path.

The parser entry still encounters constant computed keys in its handler object, so this
step alone measured flat (5451 ms before, 5470 ms after). Those static keys are the next
compilation dependency.

conformance tests passed. The remaining failure and strict-Clippy baseline are unchanged.
The new module passes strict structure checks.

Object literals now fold computed string literals, including parenthesized strings,
into the existing shape-template path. Value evaluation order, inferred function names,
duplicate-key insertion order and computed `__proto__` data properties retain their
semantics. Dynamic keys still use the interpreter. The lowering is extracted into
`bytecode/object_literal.rs`.

and 4948 ms after (about 6% less time), versus Node 228 ms and Bun 143 ms. This remains

A lazy target cache behind `Function.prototype.call` reused the existing guarded call
entry, including realm/epoch validation and weak identity pins. Target mutation, fresh
closures, overrides, proxies, strict receivers, recursion and throw-ownership tests

4998 ms) and regressed on DeltaBlue (9734 to 9917 ms). The implementation was removed;
the experiment patch and raw measurements remain in the external benchmark directory.

Keeping the bounded allocator cache warm after automatic collections, while retaining
pressure relief for explicit host collections, did not improve these workloads. Three
rotated rounds measured Djot at 5009 to 4988 ms and DeltaBlue at 9745 to 9759 ms. Median

change was removed too; allocation-cache flushing is not the material bottleneck here.

4096 operations and the callee limit from 96 to 512 changed DeltaBlue from 9725 to
10775 ms and Djot from 4979 to 5152 ms. Delaying that wider recompile to 1000 calls

remain unchanged. The next experiment targets forwarded-call elimination explicitly.

identity checks. A constructor optimizer trigger and an ownership-preserving stack
shuffle were also tested; dedicated unit checks proved ordinary calls and fast `new`

The stack-shuffle variant passed 612 unit tests and 31 integration tests.

found a correctness regression: 500 forwarded calls correctly identified their caller
before the experiment, but only the initial 110 did after inlining. The inlined body
had lost its observable legacy `function.caller` frame.

for forwarding, guard misses, constructor behavior and warmed caller reflection. A
general optimizer must preserve or reconstruct inlined frames at observable operations;

Compiled closures now share an immutable name-to-slot layout and allocate a contiguous
array of binding values for each activation. Parameters, lexical bindings, lexical
`this` and hoisted functions initialize slots directly. Structural map changes promote
the activation to the dynamic representation and invalidate cached entry addresses.
Zero generation is reserved for pristine layouts and is never reused after wrap.

ARM64 captured loads/stores/initialization can use the activation's binding-array base
and a compile-time offset. The generated path checks the scope generation and borrow
state, preserves TDZ and reference ownership, and falls back after structural mutation
or for BigInt operations. Ordinary call frames remain present.

The work is split across `interpreter/bindings.rs`, `interpreter/bindings/layout.rs`,
`bytecode/activation.rs` and `jit/captured.rs`. A callback test promotes a live compiled
activation's map and verifies subsequent captured reads/writes use the new storage.

The immutable-layout-only stage measured flat on Djot (5016 to 5019 ms) and approximately
flat on DeltaBlue (9965 to 9832 ms). With native captured access, three rotated rounds
measured Djot at 4985 to 4983 ms and DeltaBlue at 9799 to 9788 ms. No application-level
speedup is claimed. Node/Bun medians were 232/147 ms for Djot and 197/317 ms for DeltaBlue.

A separate verified closure diagnostic (100000 activations, ten reads per activation)
used 3.30 billion retired instructions versus 3.68 billion before, with maximum resident
size approximately 76 versus 110 MiB. This was one diagnostic run during unrelated build
activity, so its wall-clock timing is not used as a performance claim. Shared layouts
also enable caching deeper lexical lookup paths across fresh activations; the current
name cache only handles direct and one-parent binding resolutions.

### Guarded deeper lexical paths

Free-name reads can now cache paths of up to eight scopes. Pristine compiled scopes
are validated by their shared binding-layout identity; dynamic scopes require their
exact weak-pinned identity and structural generation. The reader walks live parent
links, validates every intervening scope against shadowing, and reads the live binding
or ordinary global data-property slot. TDZ, import redirects, with scopes, changed
shapes and accessors keep the checked resolution path. No JavaScript executes during
cache validation, and cached paths do not retain scope values or closures strongly.

ARM64 free-name cache misses now enter a dedicated guarded-path probe before the
full bytecode operation dispatcher. A successful probe transfers the cloned value
directly into the operand stack; call references also receive an undefined receiver.
A failed probe leaves the operand stack and local representation untouched and runs
the existing checked helper. BigInts keep Rust's normal clone behavior. Operation
statistics still include these hits. This is a shorter Rust helper route, not generated
machine-code validation of the complete scope path.

flat at 9729 to 9653 ms (Node/Bun 200/307 ms). Raw results are in

A separate warmed ordinary-inline caller-reflection probe reproduced an existing

### Virtual frames for inlined calls

The optimizer now records an immutable inline call chain for each bytecode location,
separately from the op stream. Checked helpers record their location before an operation
can enter JavaScript, throw or collect garbage. Native direct calls record the caller's
location before pushing the physical callee. Reflection and error-stack capture expand
that chain on demand, preserving nested `fn.caller` identities and strict-caller censoring.
The physical frame grows from 24 to 32 bytes; its native push/pop ABI and layout assertions
were updated together. Inlined bodies retain the existing restrictions on arguments,
closures and handlers; async/generator callees are explicitly excluded.

Inline targets use the existing GC bookkeeping pins when optimized code is installed.
These pins count as internal references, so inactive targets remain collectable. During
collection, active inline locations temporarily root their callees. This also keeps a
callee alive if its last ordinary reference is removed inside the inlined body, without
adding a reference-count operation to every inlined call. The locations themselves own
only weak function handles and immutable parent metadata.

An earlier explicit enter/leave-op implementation fixed reflection but disrupted five
specialized-region planning checks. It was replaced, not retained. Keeping location
metadata outside the bytecode restores all five checks. A dedicated Richards test changes
a field into a getter after warmup and verifies that the optimized region's side exit
reconstructs the inlined predicate as the getter's caller. Other tests cover nested
exceptions, strict callers, native code generation, active-callee collection safety and
collection of the same callee after return. The original warmed caller probe now passes
500/500 instead of 110/500.

Three rotated comparisons measured Djot at 4561 to 4611 ms (about one percent overhead)
and DeltaBlue at 9718 to 9693 ms (flat). Node/Bun were 230/146 ms and 195/312 ms respectively.
This is a correctness prerequisite for expanding the optimizer, not a speedup claim.

limit, GC polling, virtual-frame location and exception cleanup. The helper clones a read
result before releasing its operands, since the result can alias the key or receiver.
It still checks the live writable `__ck` marker; method replacement, proxies, incompatible
receivers and foreign-realm errors retain their checked behavior.

An initial implementation routed these reads through the shared intrinsic helper. That
version regressed Map/Set lookup medians from 360/340 to 385/365 microseconds and was
replaced. The smaller dedicated helper avoids unrelated intrinsic dispatch, dynamic
operand cleanup and constructor-state transitions. Collection reads never enter JS or
coerce their keys, so those transitions are unobservable here.

| Set build | 560 | 560 | 148.6 | 108 |
| Set lookup | 333.3 | 228 | 26.4 | 26 |

all key categories, live updates/deletions, aliasing, method replacement, receiver brands

Map.set and Set.add now have named native implementations and exact-identity JIT helpers
at their ordinary arities. After the existing depth check and GC poll, the helpers move

and new entries append after the old collision head. This avoids a separate find followed

brand failures and foreign-realm errors. Collection conformance passes 813/813 and
differential testing has 1996 agreements with four budget skips. Formatting and strict
module audits pass. Strict Clippy retains the existing 86/88 diagnostics, none in the

A fresh Djot sample taken after one second of process CPU time shows cycle collection,

An earlier sample caught dyld startup and is not evidence about engine execution. The
valid profile is `djot-after-collections-running.sample` in the external optimizer directory;

All 51 moved method bodies are unchanged. The public Props facade and probed JIT layout

=== examples/djot-parser/README.md # Djot parser on lumen Parses [Djot](https://djot.net) markup to an AST and renders it to HTML with `@djot/djot`, a pure-JS parser — no native code. `@djot/djot` is CommonJS, so it's default-imported and destructured (lumen exposes a CJS module's `module.exports` as the ESM default). ```sh npm install ../../target/release/lumen-cli parse.mjs ``` === examples/ejs/README.md # yt-dlp/ejs on lumen [yt-dlp/ejs](https://github.com/yt-dlp/ejs) is yt-dlp's external JavaScript challenge solver: it bundles **meriyah** (a JavaScript parser written in JavaScript) and **astring** (a code generator), parses YouTube's multi-megabyte player source, transforms it, and solves the sig/nsig challenges. As a workload it is brutal on an engine's string implementation — a scanner reading a ~3 MB source one `charCodeAt` at a time, tokens `slice`d out by the thousand, and the transformed source rebuilt through repeated string concatenation. That made it a perfect stress test: [issue #12](https://github.com/lucid-softworks/lumen/issues/12) reported the benchmark below taking **55.8 minutes** on lumen. ## Running it ```sh ./fetch.sh # downloads the benchmark bundle (solver + embedded player + challenges) ./bench.sh # times it on lumen (and node/bun/qjs when installed) ``` The bundle is the exact reproducer from issue #12 — the ejs core solver with a player and two `n`-challenges baked in; it prints the solved challenge results as JSON. To build a fresh bundle from upstream instead, see yt-dlp/ejs's own build docs (`rollup` via `pnpm`/`deno`/`bun`; release assets ship the prebuilt `yt.solver.core.js`). ## Numbers (Apple M-series, 2026-07) | runtime | time | notes | |---|---:|---| | node 22 | 0.44 s | | | bun 1.3 | 0.47 s | | | qjs (quickjs-ng, brew) | 3.4 s | (the 8.2 s in issue #12 was a slower machine) | | **lumen** (`--tier=jit`) | **8.7 s** | was **55.8 min** at the time of issue #12 | What the 55.8 minutes was made of, in the order it fell: 1. **Per-call UTF-16 materialization** — every `charCodeAt`/`s[i]`/`.length` walked or converted the *whole* UTF-8 string per call: O(n²) for meriyah's scanner. Fixed with a pointer-keyed cache of each string's UTF-16 view (ASCII indexes bytes directly). 55.8 min → 2.7 min. 2. **Double-copy concatenation** — each `a + b` copied the accumulation twice. 2.7 min → 82 s. 3. **The append loop itself** — `s += x` on immutable exactly-sized strings is inherently O(n²). The engine string is now a thin refcounted buffer *with spare capacity* (`LStr`, the design original QuickJS uses), and the fused `obj.k += v` op appends **in place** when the accumulator is uniquely referenced — astring's `write()` becomes amortized O(1). 82 s → 16 s. 4. **Compiled-tier coverage and inline caches** — object-destructuring declarations (at block *and* function-body level), simple parameter defaults, optional chains (`a?.b`, `r?.m(x)`), `for…of` (with exact IteratorClose semantics on break/return/throw), and template literals now compile; and the inline property caches are guarded by a *per-object* side-table flag instead of a global latch (one `Uint8Array` existing no longer disables every cache in the program). meriyah's parser now runs almost entirely on the compiled tiers. → 8.7 s. (Chasing this also surfaced and fixed a real compiled-tier bug: `break` out of a `try` block leaked its handler, silently swallowing unrelated later throws.) Addons that call an unimplemented `napi_*` function fail at load with a clear error naming the missing symbol (the library is opened with `RTLD_NOW`, so unresolved symbols surface immediately rather than mid-call). === examples/preact-ssr/README.md # Preact SSR on lumen Server-side renders a Preact component with `preact-render-to-string`, served over `node:http` (ESM). ```sh npm install ../../target/release/lumen-cli server.mjs # http://localhost:3000 ``` === examples/react-jsx-ssr/README.md # React JSX / TSX SSR on lumen Server-side render React components with `react-dom/server`'s `renderToString`. ## `.jsx` — runs natively lumen's runtime transpiles JSX to `React.createElement` calls itself (a from-scratch JSX transformer, no build tool), so a `.jsx` file runs directly: ```sh npm install ../../target/release/lumen-cli app.jsx ``` ```

hello

world 🌏

``` ## `.tsx` — via esbuild TypeScript *type* stripping is not built in, so a `.tsx` file (with `interface`, `React.FC<…>` annotations) is transpiled with esbuild — which itself runs on lumen — before executing: ```sh ../../target/release/lumen-cli render.mjs app.tsx ``` `app.tsx` (a recursive component) renders a nested tree and reports its SSR time. ## How it works - **`.jsx` natively:** the runtime lowers `
hi
` to `React.createElement("div", { a: x }, "hi")` in a single scan (`crates/lumen-runtime/src/jsx.rs`) — classic runtime, so the component's own `import React` supplies the factory. The engine's parser is untouched (JSX text with apostrophes would break an up-front lexer), and the transform runs as a pre-pass on `.jsx` sources. - **`.tsx` via esbuild:** `render.mjs` runs esbuild's `tsx` loader (which strips types *and* lowers JSX). `ESBUILD_WORKER_THREADS=0` selects esbuild's subprocess path, since lumen has no worker threads. - **Module resolution:** the transpiled code keeps `import React` / `import { renderToString }` as ESM imports; lumen resolves them from `node_modules` and follows `react-dom/server`'s CommonJS re-export chain (`server.js → server.node.js → cjs/*.js`) to expose `renderToString` as a named ESM export. For a pure-`React.createElement`, no-transpile version served over `node:http`, see `examples/react-ssr`. === examples/react-ssr/README.md # React SSR on lumen Server-side renders a React component tree to HTML with `react-dom/server`'s `renderToString`, served over `node:http`. Uses `React.createElement` directly, so there's no JSX build step. ```sh npm install ../../target/release/lumen-cli server.js # http://localhost:3000 ``` === examples/vite-app/README.md # Vite build on lumen A real [Vite](https://vitejs.dev) production build (`vite build`) running on lumen — bundling with Rollup's **native N-API addon**, transforming with **esbuild** (a spawned service child), and writing a hashed, minified bundle. ```sh npm install ../../target/release/lumen-cli node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js build ``` Expected output: ``` vite vX building for production... ✓ 3 modules transformed. dist/index.html 0.14 kB │ gzip: 0.14 kB dist/assets/index-*.js 0.77 kB │ gzip: 0.53 kB ✓ built in ~190ms ``` The process builds, writes `dist/`, and exits cleanly. ## What this exercises This is one of the most demanding npm workloads, and it drives a lot of lumen at once: - **Native addons** — `@rollup/rollup-.node` is `dlopen`ed and run through lumen's from-scratch N-API implementation (`crates/lumen-node/src/napi.rs`). - **child_process + esbuild** — esbuild runs as a long-lived service subprocess; lumen's `child.ref()`/`unref()` let the build wait for transforms yet still exit when done. - **ESM ↔ CommonJS interop** — Vite and its deps mix ESM and CJS; lumen statically discovers a CJS module's named exports so `import { parse } from './native.js'` links. - **The node: surface** — `fs` (real stat metadata), `path`, `url`, `crypto`, `zlib` (real gzip size reporting), `dns`, `v8`, `worker_threads`, `process`, and more. === examples/wintertc-showcase/README.md # WinterTC showcase A single script touring lumen's implementation of the WinterTC **Minimum Common API** (53/53 interfaces): encoding, `structuredClone`, `URL`/`URLPattern`, `crypto`,   I've built the compression module in `/workspace/src/compress/`. All five encoders reproduce the original byte-for-byte, and all decoders match its outputs and exact error messages on every case I tested. It compiles warning-free under the workspace's own `Cargo.toml` (std only, no `unsafe`, edition 2021), and its 12 unit tests pass in release and debug builds. I never built in `/workspace` and never ran `compile.sh`; checks ran on a copy under `/tmp`.
  
  **Files:** `mod.rs` (API plus the documentation you'll implement the JS side from), `checksum.rs`, `inflate.rs`, `deflate.rs`, `brotli_dec.rs`, `brotli_enc.rs`, `brotli_dict.bin`, `zstd_dec.rs`, `zstd_enc.rs`. I got the brotli dictionary by decoding crafted streams with node's decoder; its SHA-256 matches the published RFC value.
  
  **API:** your spec's functions (`crc32`, `adler32`, deflate/zlib/gzip encode and decode, `unzip_decode`, brotli and zstd), plus:
  - **`Codec`:** maps each stream class and each `CompressionStream` format to its codec.
  - **`BufferedCodec`:** buffers written chunks and runs the codec once at the end.
  - **`ZLIB_CONSTANTS`:** `zlib.constants` with the original's 170 keys, order and values.
  - **`CodecError`:** `message` is the original's exact text. The original's errors have no `code` or `errno`, so `code` is always `""` and `errno` always `0`; don't expose them to JS.
  
  **How I checked it**
  - **Encoders:** 825 outputs across all formats (empty to ~1 MB, text, random, runs, matches farther than 32 KB), plus about 980 extra brotli cases. All identical.
  - **Decoders:** over 30,000 crafted, fuzzed and valid inputs (node, libzstd, Python zlib), compared directly against the original. All identical, including all 40 bundled assets.
  
  **What you need to know for the bindings** (full detail with sample outputs is in the `mod.rs` doc comment):
  - **Options are never read.** That covers level, strategy, windowBits, `dictionary`, `info`, `maxOutputLength`, `chunkSize` and all brotli/zstd params. Nothing is validated and nothing throws for bad options.
  - **The original is lax in specific ways:**
    - **zlib wrapper:** neither Adler-32 nor FCHECK is checked.
    - **gzip:** CRC and length are not checked. Only the first member is decoded and trailing garbage is ignored.
    - **unzip:** `unzipSync` is just gunzip, with no zlib auto-detection.
    - **brotli:** large-window streams are rejected.
    - **zstd:** checksums are verified and trailing bytes are an error.
  - **The compressors are weak:**
    - **deflate:** one fixed-Huffman block with greedy matching. Matches farther than 32 KB produce corrupt streams; I reproduce that deliberately.
    - **brotli:** literal-only, or stored.
    - **zstd:** raw and RLE blocks only.
  - **Async functions** (`zlib.gzip(buf, cb)` etc.) run the job in a single microtask and never throw synchronously.
  - **Streams and Compression/DecompressionStream** buffer all input and emit exactly one output chunk at `end()`/`close()`. The exact JS class model, event order and error behaviour are in the doc comment.
  - **1 MiB cap:** the original's engine refuses any typed array over 1 MiB (`RangeError: Invalid typed array length`). That caps every result; this module has no such limit.
  
  **Known differences and untestable areas**
  - **`dictionary` argument:** on `inflate_raw`/`zlib_decode` it is an extension the original doesn't have; pass `None` to match it.
  - **Inputs above 1 MiB:** these can't be compared against the original. Brotli inputs over 16 MiB are split into several meta-blocks (node decodes them correctly), and the zstd 8-byte content-size field is written per spec.
  - **Decompression bombs:** there is no output cap, so a malicious input can make the decoders allocate very large outputs.
  
  I used four subagents for the JS-API, stream and decoder-error investigations, then spot-checked their key claims myself. One of them once printed `zlib.Gunzip` with `console.log`, which showed the class source. It disclosed this and re-confirmed every related claim with black-box tests, and I didn't use that output.
  
  Scratch work is all under `/tmp`: `compress_dev`, `compress_final`, `ws_check`, `x`, `agent_*`.

  - **gzip:** CRC and length are not checked. Only the first member is decoded and trailing garbage is ignored.

  - **brotli:** large-window streams are rejected.
  - **zstd:** checksums are verified and trailing bytes are an error.

- **Decompression bombs:** there is no output cap, so a malicious input can make the decoders allocate very large outputs.

I've written `/workspace/src/datetime.rs` (std only, no `unsafe`, about 3,700 lines, most of it data tables). It builds warning-free as a private module of a 2021-edition bin crate in debug and release, and its 8 unit tests pass. Every differential corpus run against the original matched exactly:

| What | Cases | Mismatches |
|---|---|---|
| Timestamps across the full range: fixed string formats and getters | ~7.5k | 0 |
| `Date.UTC` argument tuples | ~3.6k | 0 |
| Parse strings (fuzzed and realistic), through both `Date.parse` and `new Date(str)` | ~90k | 0 |
| Locale / option / time-zone cases | ~95k | 0 |

## Answers to your specific questions
- **Local time zone:** always UTC. I re-checked: `TZ` is ignored for 8 different values. `/etc/localtime` here is UTC and I couldn't swap it (no namespaces), so that one input is untested. `local_tza()` returns 0.
- **NaN:** `String(new Date(NaN))` and `new Date(8.64e15+1)` both print `"Invalid Date"`. `new Date(NaN).toISOString()` throws `RangeError: Invalid time value`, and `toJSON` returns `null`. Calling a Date method on a non-Date throws `TypeError: this is not a Date object`.
- **Years:** `toString`/`toUTCString` use at least 4 digits with a sign for negatives (`-0001`, `0000`, `12345`, `-271821`). `toISOString` uses `±YYYYYY` outside 0..9999.
- **Your side of `new Date(y, m)` / `Date.UTC`:** map years 0..99 to 1900+, TimeClip after `make_date`, and return NaN for `Date.UTC()` with no arguments. `setFullYear`, `setUTCFullYear` and `setYear` start from +0 on an invalid date; the other setters stay NaN.
- **`make_day`:** returns NaN when `year + floor(month/12)` is beyond ±300000. That's the original's limit (V8 uses ±1e6).

## Parsing — the big surprise
- **`new Date(string)` only accepts ISO-like strings.** Legacy strings, even the original's own `toString()` output, give Invalid Date in the constructor, while `Date.parse` accepts them. So you must call `parse_for_constructor` (already clipped) for the constructor and `parse` for `Date.parse`.
- **Legacy results are not TimeClip'ed.** `Date.parse("Sep 14 275760")` returns `8640000086400000`, and the arithmetic wraps like 64-bit integers, which I reproduce bit-for-bit.
- **Strict ISO** doesn't range-check fields: `2020-13-01` is 2021-01-01, `2020-02-30` is March 1, and `T24:00:01` or `T25:00` overflow. `T10` and `T10.5` are accepted. `+0100`, `+01`, lowercase `t`/`z` and a leading U+FEFF are rejected.
- **Space-separated form:** `2020-1-2 3:4`, `202 03:04` and `…+0100` are all accepted because a second, looser parser handles strings with a space in them.
- **Legacy formats:** month is read from the first three letters (`Septembre`, `Junk` count). AM/PM and zone abbreviations like EST are silently ignored, so `"Mar 7 2020 1:00 PM"` is 01:00. Parentheses are just separators, not comments. Two-digit years stay as written (`Mar 7 20` is year 20). A signed number sets the year: `"… 10:00 +0200"` gives year 200. `10:20:30.5` loses its seconds. Slash forms like `2020/03/07` and `03/07/2020` are NaN.
- **Crashes:** the original aborts the whole process on a few odd inputs, e.g. `"2376 x-5é("`. We return NaN instead.

## Locale formatting
- **Defaults:** `"1/1/1970, 12:00:00 AM"`, `"1/1/1970"`, `"12:00:00 AM"`; default locale `en`, zone `UTC`.
- **It's not CLDR**, it's a small built-in table. Twenty-one languages have data; everything else falls back to `en`, and `en-GB` prints like `en-US`.
- **Only some things are localised:** date order and separator, month and era names, the default 24-hour clock for non-`en` locales, and Arabic digits for `ar`. Weekdays, AM/PM, day periods and zone names are always English, so `de` gives `"Saturday, März 7, 2020"`.
- **Other quirks:** `{weekday:'long'}` alone gives `"Saturday, "`, and `{year, month:'short'}` gives `"Mar, 2020"`.
- **What's covered:** all options, `dateStyle`/`timeStyle`, `hour12`/`hourCycle`, `-u-ca/-nu/-hc` extensions, every decimal numbering system, `formatToParts`, `resolvedOptions`, and the original's exact error messages.
- **Time zones:** `UTC`, fixed offsets, and all 600 IANA names, read at run time from `/usr/share/zoneinfo`. Small embedded tables reproduce the original's quirks:
  - no DST after 2037;
  - the short zone name always shows the offset at the epoch, so New York in July still prints `GMT-5`;
  - odd long names (`Europe/London` prints as `Europe/Guernsey`);
  - its older data for Morocco, Alberta/Manitoba and Dublin 1925.
- **What to call:** build a `DateTimeFormatOptions` (`set`, `set_hour12`, `set_fractional_second_digits`), call `canonicalize_locale_list` first so locale errors win over option errors, then `to_locale_string` / `to_locale_date_string` / `to_locale_time_string`, or use `DateTimeFormat` directly. Errors come back as `DateTimeError { kind: Range | Type, message }`.
- **What you handle:** the option read order and the error messages for `null` options, bad locale-list entries and so on. They're in the doc comment at the top of the file.

## Known gaps
- **Calendars:** gregory, iso8601, buddhist, roc and japanese are implemented. The other calendars the original supports (islamic, chinese, hebrew, persian and others) are reported in `resolvedOptions` but formatted as Gregorian.
- **Not implemented:** `formatRange` and `formatRangeToParts`.
- **Locale canonicalization is partial:** only a few aliases (`sh`, `cmn`, `iw`, `840`→`US` and similar). This only affects the tag strings that come back for unusual tags.
- **`/usr/share/zoneinfo` dependency:** time zones need it on the test machine. Without it, IANA names throw "invalid time zone" while `UTC` and offsets still work.

// Bytecode definitions shared by compiler and VM.

use crate::ast::FuncKind;
use crate::value::*;
use std::rc::Rc;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum BindKind {
    Var,
    Let,
    Const,
    Class,
    Function,
    Param,
    CatchParam,
    /// internal bindings: this, arguments, new.target, home, private names
    Internal,
    /// the name of a named function expression (immutable, silently ignores writes in sloppy)
    FuncName,
    Import,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct ScopeInfo {
    pub names: Vec<JsStr>,
    pub kinds: Vec<BindKind>,
    pub is_function: bool,
}

impl ScopeInfo {
    pub fn find(&self, name: &JsStr) -> Option<usize> {
        self.names.iter().position(|n| n == name)
    }
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MethodTarget {
    Proto,
    Ctor,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MKind {
    Method,
    Getter,
    Setter,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct TemplateData {
    pub cooked: Vec<Option<JsStr>>,
    pub raw: Vec<JsStr>,
    pub id: usize,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
pub enum Op {
    // constants
    Undef,
    Null,
    True,
    False,
    Int(i32),
    Const(u32),
    Empty,
    // stack
    Pop,
    Dup,
    Dup2,
    Swap,
    /// [a b c] -> [c a b]
    Rot3,
    /// [a b c d] -> [d a b c]
    Rot4,
    /// copy the value n below the top: [.. x a1..an] -> [.. x a1..an x]
    Pick(u16),
    // locals / env
    GetLocal(u32),
    GetLocalChk(u32, u32),
    SetLocal(u32),
    InitLocal(u32),
    ClearLocal(u32),
    GetEnv(u16, u32),
    GetEnvChk(u16, u32, u32),
    SetEnv(u16, u32),
    SetEnvChk(u16, u32, u32),
    InitEnv(u16, u32),
    GetName(u32),
    SetName(u32),
    TypeofName(u32),
    DeleteName(u32),
    /// pushes [this, func] for a call to an identifier (with-scope aware)
    GetNameCall(u32),
    GetGlobal(u32),
    SetGlobal(u32),
    TypeofGlobal(u32),
    /// declare global var (name, is_function)
    DeclareGlobalVar(u32),
    DeclareGlobalFunc(u32),
    DeclareGlobalLex(u32, bool),
    InitGlobalLex(u32),
    PushScope(u32),
    PopScope,
    CopyScope,
    PushWith,
    ThrowConst(u32),
    // function frame
    This,
    ThisChk,
    SetThis,
    NewTarget,
    GetArg(u32),
    GetRest(u32),
    CreateArguments(bool),
    Callee,
    Home,
    // properties
    GetProp(u32),
    GetPropOpt(u32),
    GetElem,
    SetProp(u32),
    SetElem,
    DeleteProp(u32),
    DeleteElem,
    GetSuper(u32),
    GetSuperElem,
    SetSuper(u32),
    SetSuperElem,
    GetPrivate,
    SetPrivate,
    PrivateIn,
    /// [obj] -> [obj, obj.key]  (for method calls: leaves this then func)
    GetMethod(u32),
    GetMethodElem,
    ToPropKey,
    // literals
    NewObject,
    NewArray(u32),
    ArrayPush,
    ArrayHole,
    ArraySpread,
    DefineField(u32),
    DefineFieldComputed,
    DefineAccessor(u32, MKind),
    DefineAccessorComputed(MKind),
    CopyDataProps,
    /// [target source excludedKeys...(n)] object rest
    CopyDataPropsExcept(u32),
    SetProtoLit,
    RegExp(u32),
    Template(u32),
    // functions & classes
    Closure(u32),
    /// [home] -> [home, closure]
    Method(u32),
    SetFunctionName(u8),
    /// [heritage?] -> [F, proto]
    CreateClass(u32, bool),
    /// [F proto (key)?] method definition
    DefineMethod(u32, MethodTarget, MKind, u32),
    DefineMethodComputed(MethodTarget, MKind, u32),
    /// [F proto key?] -> instance field registration (key idx or computed when u32::MAX)
    AddField(u32, u32, bool),
    AddFieldComputed(u32, bool),
    /// [F proto sym] private method/accessor for instances
    AddPrivateMethod(u32, MKind, bool),
    /// [F proto] run static field initializer with key
    StaticField(u32, u32),
    StaticFieldComputed(u32),
    /// [F proto sym]
    StaticPrivateField(u32),
    StaticBlock(u32),
    NewPrivateName(u32),
    // operators
    Add,
    Sub,
    Mul,
    Div,
    Mod,
    Exp,
    Shl,
    Shr,
    UShr,
    BitAnd,
    BitOr,
    BitXor,
    Eq,
    Ne,
    StrictEq,
    StrictNe,
    Lt,
    Le,
    Gt,
    Ge,
    In,
    InstanceOf,
    Neg,
    Plus,
    Not,
    BitNot,
    Typeof,
    Void,
    Inc,
    Dec,
    ToNumeric,
    ToStr,
    // control
    Jump(u32),
    JumpIfFalse(u32),
    JumpIfTrue(u32),
    JumpIfFalseKeep(u32),
    JumpIfTrueKeep(u32),
    JumpIfNullishKeep(u32),
    JumpIfNotNullishKeep(u32),
    /// jump if top is undefined (pops if not jumping? no: always pops)
    JumpIfNotUndef(u32),
    /// jumps if top is null or undefined (pops)
    JumpIfNullish(u32),
    Return,
    TryStart(u32),
    TryEnd,
    Throw,
    ThrowRef(u32),
    ThrowType(u32),
    // calls (stack: this, func, args...)
    Call(u32, u32),
    CallArray(u32),
    CallEval(u32),
    CallEvalArray,
    New(u32),
    NewArray_,
    SuperCall(u32),
    SuperCallArray,
    // iteration
    GetIterator,
    GetAsyncIterator,
    /// [iter next] -> [iter next value] or jump when done
    IterNext(u32),
    IterClose,
    IterCloseSilent,
    /// destructuring: [iter next done] -> [iter next done value]
    IterValue,
    IterRest,
    IterDone,
    ForInStart,
    ForInNext(u32),
    // generators / async
    Yield,
    /// after resume from yield: handles throw/return; return jumps to target
    GenResume(u32),
    Await,
    /// [iter next received] delegation step; done -> push value, continue
    YieldStar(u32, bool),
    AsyncIterValue,
    /// convert iterator result of async iteration: [iter next result] -> value or jump when done
    AsyncIterCheck(u32),
    // misc
    Debugger,
    ImportMeta,
    DynamicImport,
    Nop,
    /// [obj] -> [obj] throws if not object (iterator results etc.)
    CheckObj,
    /// push undefined if top is Empty (used by super calls)
    /// dispose resources at scope exit (using declarations)
    AddDisposable(bool),
    DisposeScope(u32),
}

pub struct FunctionCode {
    pub name: JsStr,
    pub ops: Vec<Op>,
    pub consts: Vec<Value>,
    pub keys: Vec<PropKey>,
    pub funcs: Vec<Rc<FunctionCode>>,
    pub scopes: Vec<Rc<ScopeInfo>>,
    pub templates: Vec<Rc<TemplateData>>,
    pub regexps: Vec<(JsStr, JsStr)>,
    pub strings: Vec<JsStr>,
    pub nlocals: u32,
    pub length: u32,
    pub kind: FuncKind,
    pub is_async: bool,
    pub is_generator: bool,
    pub strict: bool,
    pub source: Rc<str>,
    pub src_start: usize,
    pub src_end: usize,
    pub is_arrow: bool,
    pub has_simple_params: bool,
    pub line: u32,
    /// a function with no own `prototype` (methods, arrows, async functions, ...)
    pub no_prototype: bool,
    pub class_source: bool,
    /// name set from a class/declaration (affects toString for default ctor)
    pub is_default_ctor: bool,
    pub is_script: bool,
    pub is_module: bool,
}

impl FunctionCode {
    pub fn is_constructor(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(self.kind, FuncKind::Normal | FuncKind::ClassConstructor | FuncKind::DerivedConstructor)
            && !self.is_async
            && !self.is_generator
    }
    pub fn source_text(&self) -> String {
        if self.is_default_ctor {
            return String::new();
        }
        self.source.chars().skip(self.src_start).take(self.src_end.saturating_sub(self.src_start)).collect()
    }
}

impl std::fmt::Debug for FunctionCode {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        writeln!(f, "function {} (locals={}, strict={})", self.name, self.nlocals, self.strict)?;
        for (i, op) in self.ops.iter().enumerate() {
            writeln!(f, "  {:4} {:?}", i, op)?;
        }
        for (i, func) in self.funcs.iter().enumerate() {
            writeln!(f, "-- nested #{}:", i)?;
            write!(f, "{:?}", func)?;
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

pub struct FunctionCode {
    pub name: JsStr,
    pub ops: Vec<Op>,
    pub consts: Vec<Value>,
    pub keys: Vec<PropKey>,
    pub funcs: Vec<Rc<FunctionCode>>,
    pub scopes: Vec<Rc<ScopeInfo>>,
    pub templates: Vec<Rc<TemplateData>>,
    pub regexps: Vec<(JsStr, JsStr)>,
    pub strings: Vec<JsStr>,
    pub nlocals: u32,
    pub length: u32,
    pub kind: FuncKind,
    pub is_async: bool,
    pub is_generator: bool,
    pub strict: bool,
    pub source: Rc<str>,
    pub src_start: usize,
    pub src_end: usize,
    pub is_arrow: bool,
    pub has_simple_params: bool,
    pub line: u32,
    /// a function with no own `prototype` (methods, arrows, async functions, ...)
    pub no_prototype: bool,
    pub class_source: bool,
    /// name set from a class/declaration (affects toString for default ctor)
    pub is_default_ctor: bool,
    pub is_script: bool,
    pub is_module: bool,
}

impl FunctionCode {
    pub fn is_constructor(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(self.kind, FuncKind::Normal | FuncKind::ClassConstructor | FuncKind::DerivedConstructor)
            && !self.is_async
            && !self.is_generator
    }
    pub fn source_text(&self) -> String {
        if self.is_default_ctor {
            return String::new();
        }
        self.source.chars().skip(self.src_start).take(self.src_end.saturating_sub(self.src_start)).collect()
    }
}

impl std::fmt::Debug for FunctionCode {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        writeln!(f, "function {} (locals={}, strict={})", self.name, self.nlocals, self.strict)?;
        for (i, op) in self.ops.iter().enumerate() {
            writeln!(f, "  {:4} {:?}", i, op)?;
        }
        for (i, func) in self.funcs.iter().enumerate() {
            writeln!(f, "-- nested #{}:", i)?;
            write!(f, "{:?}", func)?;
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

# Guide for subagents working on the lumen reimplementation

## The project
We are reimplementing, from scratch in Rust (std only, NO external crates), a JavaScript engine +
Node/Bun-like runtime called "lumen" (CLI `lumen-cli`). The ORIGINAL compiled binary is at
`/workspace/executable` (symlink `/tmp/orig`). Our reimplementation lives in the git repo `/workspace`
(you will be working in your own git worktree copy of it). Hidden tests will run JS programs through
both binaries and compare stdout, stderr and exit code EXACTLY, so fidelity to the original's
observable behavior (output formats, error messages, property orders, edge cases) is the goal.

## Rules (strict)
- You may RUN the original (`/tmp/orig file.js`, `/tmp/orig -e 'code'`) to observe behavior.
- You MUST NOT disassemble/decompile/read the original binary's bytes, use strace/ltrace/gdb on it,
  search the internet, or download anything. No network is available anyway.
- Do not copy JS source code text of the original's internal modules verbatim (some functions print
  their JS source via `String(fn)`; you may observe *behavior*, but write your own Rust implementation).
- Write Rust (std only). Keep any scratch scripts (shell/python/JS test files) OUTSIDE the repo, e.g.
  under `/tmp/<yourname>/`. Do not add non-Rust code files to the repo.
- Only edit the files assigned to you. If a core-engine bug blocks you, work around it in your files
  if possible and describe the bug precisely in your final report (file/function, repro JS). If you
  absolutely must touch a shared file, keep the change minimal and list it in your report.
- Never run `/workspace/compile.sh` and never write to `/workspace/executable`.
- Build with `cargo build --release` in YOUR worktree (binary: `target/release/lumen`). Commit your
  work in your worktree with clear messages when done (and at milestones).
- `console.log` in lumen prints values via `String(v)` (objects print as `[object Object]`), so when
  probing the original use JSON.stringify or explicit string building.

## Engine architecture (what you need to write builtins)
Key modules (in `src/`): `value.rs` (Value, JsStr, Sym, PropKey), `object.rs` (Obj, ObjKind, Prop,
PropDesc, Args, NativeFn, flags WRITABLE/ENUMERABLE/CONFIGURABLE, WEC, WC), `vm.rs` (Vm, JsResult,
calls, errors, frames, Job), `props.rs` (property internal methods on Vm), `ops.rs` (conversions),
`realm.rs` (intrinsics + helpers to define builtins), `builtins/*` (ECMAScript builtins),
`runtime/*` (node/web runtime), `runtime/mod.rs` (Host state, event loop), `modules.rs` (ESM).

### Values
```rust
enum Value { Undefined, Null, Bool(bool), Num(f64), Str(JsStr), Sym(Sym), BigInt(Rc<BigInt>), Obj(Obj), Empty /*internal*/ }
JsStr::from_str("x"), s.to_rust_string(), s.units() -> &[u16] (UTF-16), JsStr::from_units(vec), JsStr::concat(&a,&b)
Value::str("x"), Value::Num(1.0), v.is_undefined(), v.is_nullish(), v.as_obj() -> Option<&Obj>, v.truthy(), v.is_callable()
PropKey::from_str("name"), PropKey::Str(js), PropKey::Sym(sym), PropKey::from_index(i)
```
### Natives
```rust
type NativeFn = fn(&mut Vm, &Args) -> JsResult<Value>;   // JsResult<T> = Result<T, Value /*thrown*/>
// Args: a.this (Value), a.args (&[Value]), a.arg(i) -> Value (undefined if missing), a.callee (&Obj),
//       a.new_target (Option<Obj>, Some when called with `new`), a.slot(i) -> captured data (see native_closure)
vm.native_fn("name", length, f) -> Obj                         // function object
vm.native_closure("name", length, f, vec![slot0, slot1]) -> Obj // with captured Values (read via a.slot(i))
vm.def_method(&obj, "name", length, f) -> Obj                    // non-enumerable writable configurable method
vm.def_getter(&obj, "name", f); vm.def_accessor(&obj, "name", getter, setter)
vm.native_ctor("Name", length, f, &proto) -> Obj   // constructor; links proto.constructor & ctor.prototype
// In a constructor native: let p = vm.proto_from_nt(&a.new_target, &fallback_proto)?; Obj::new(Some(p), kind)
vm.make_ctor(&fobj)  // mark a native fn as constructible
vm.def_global("Name", Value::Obj(o)); vm.set_tag(&obj, "Tag") // Symbol.toStringTag
```
### Objects
```rust
vm.new_object() -> Obj (plain, Object.prototype); vm.obj_from(vec![("k", v), ...]) -> Obj (enumerable props)
vm.new_array(vec![...]) -> Obj; Obj::new(proto: Option<Obj>, ObjKind::Ordinary)
o.set_str("k", v, WEC); o.set_prop(PropKey, v, flags); o.get_own_str("k") -> Option<Value> (own data only)
o.borrow() / o.borrow_mut()  (RefCell — never hold a borrow across a call into JS!)
// custom native state: Obj::new(Some(proto), ObjKind::Host(Box::new(MyState{..}))) and later
//   if let ObjKind::Host(h) = &o.borrow().kind { if let Some(s) = h.downcast_ref::<MyState>() {..} }
//   (use Cell/RefCell inside MyState for mutation)
crate::runtime::reorder_enum(vm, &obj, &["a","b",...]) // force enumerable key order (missing -> noop fns)
```
### Property access / conversions (all on `vm`)
```rust
vm.get(&obj, &key, &receiver_value)?; vm.get_str(&obj, "name")?; vm.get_prop_of(&value, &key)? (works on primitives)
vm.set_prop_of(&value, key, v, /*strict*/ true)?; vm.create_data_property(&obj, key, v)?
vm.has_property(&obj, &key)?; vm.delete(&obj, &key)?; vm.own_property_keys(&obj)?; vm.enumerable_own_keys(&obj)?
vm.to_string(&v)? -> JsStr; vm.to_number(&v)?; vm.to_object(&v)?; vm.to_property_key(&v)?; vm.to_index(&v)?
vm.to_integer_or_infinity(&v)?; vm.to_int32/to_uint32; vm.to_primitive(&v, crate::ops::Hint::Default)?
crate::runtime::display_value(vm, &v) -> String   // what console.log prints for a value
crate::runtime::util::inspect_value(vm, &v, depth)? -> String  // util.inspect
crate::runtime::util::describe_received(vm, &v) -> String // Node-style "Received type number (5)"
vm.call(&f, this, &args)?; vm.construct(&ctor, &args, None)?; vm.iterate_to_vec(&iterable)?
crate::builtins::array::array_like_to_vec(vm, &v)?
```
### Errors
```rust
return vm.throw_type("message");   // also throw_range, throw_ref, throw_syntax, throw_error("URIError", msg)
let e = vm.make_error("TypeError", "msg"); if let Value::Obj(o) = &e { o.set_prop(PropKey::from_str("code"), Value::str("ERR_X"), WEC); } return Err(e);
```
### Promises / async / event loop
```rust
let cap = vm.new_promise_capability_intrinsic(); // Capability { promise, resolve, reject }
vm.call(&cap.resolve, Value::Undefined, &[v])?; return Ok(cap.promise);
crate::builtins::promise::promise_then(vm, &promise_obj, on_fulfilled_fn_value, on_rejected_fn_value)?
crate::builtins::promise::perform_then_internal(vm, &p, Handler::Native(f, data), Handler::Native(g, data), None)
   // f: fn(&mut Vm, Value /*result*/, &Value /*data*/) -> JsResult<Value>
vm.jobs.push_back(crate::vm::Job::Callback(f, args));      // microtask
vm.host.callbacks.push_back((f, args));                     // macrotask (setImmediate-like queue)
crate::runtime::timers::add_timer(vm, cb, delay_ms, args, repeat) -> id
crate::runtime::spawn_op(vm, move || { /* runs on a thread, return T: Send */ }, move |vm, t: T| { /* back on loop thread */ });
   // keeps the event loop alive until `then` runs. Never move Values/Objs into the thread closure.
```
### Buffers / bytes
```rust
crate::runtime::buffer::new_buffer_value(vm, bytes)?      // Node Buffer (Uint8Array subclass)
crate::runtime::buffer::bytes_of(vm, &v)?                  // bytes of string(utf8)/Buffer/TypedArray/ArrayBuffer/array
crate::builtins::typedarray::ta_bytes(&obj)                // bytes of TypedArray/ArrayBuffer/DataView
crate::builtins::typedarray::typed_array_from_bytes(vm, bytes) -> Obj  // plain Uint8Array
crate::runtime::buffer::{encode_string, decode_bytes, norm_encoding}   // node encodings
crate::runtime::encoding::{base64_encode, base64_decode_strict, hex_encode, utf16_to_utf8, utf8_to_utf16}
```
### EventEmitter helpers
`crate::runtime::events::{install_methods(vm,&proto), init_emitter(vm,&obj), emit_event(vm,&this_value,&Value::str("evt"),&args)?}`
and `create_module(vm)` returns the EventEmitter constructor (also cached via `crate::runtime::node::builtin_module(vm, "events")?`).

### Module registry
`crate::runtime::node::builtin_module(vm, "name")? -> Option<Value>` returns (cached) exports of a node
builtin (used by `require`, `import`, `process.getBuiltinModule`). The dispatch is in
`runtime/node.rs::builtin_module`; your module's `create_module(vm, name)` is already wired.
Globals are installed by `setup(vm)` functions called from `runtime/mod.rs::setup_runtime`.

## Testing
Write JS test files under `/tmp/<yourname>/` and compare outputs of `/tmp/orig` vs your build:
`/tmp/orig t.js > o1 2> e1; echo $? ; target/release/lumen t.js > o2 2> e2; echo $?; diff o1 o2; diff e1 e2`.
Cover typical usage first (what a test-writer would exercise), then edge cases and error messages.
Note process.argv[0]/timings legitimately differ.

    - Errors print their stack; an invalid Date prints `Invalid Date`. The top-level call can return a non-string value (e.g. an error whose `stack` is a number).
    - Deep nesting throws "Maximum call stack size exceeded" at about the same depth as the original (within one level).
